The term, which may be derived from the name of a Swiss political leader, the Genevan burgomaster Besançon Hugues, was in common use by around 1550. Huguenot was frequently used in reference to those of the Reformed Church of France from the time of the Protestant Reformation. By contrast, the Protestant populations of eastern France, in Alsace, Moselle, and Montbéliard, were mainly Lutherans.

In his Encyclopedia of Protestantism, Hans Hillerbrand wrote that on the eve of the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre in 1572, the Huguenot community made up as much as 10% of the French population. By 1600, it declined to 7–8%, and was reduced further late in the century after the return of persecution under Louis XIV, who instituted the Dragonnades to forcibly convert Protestants, and then finally revoked all Protestant rights in his Edict of Fontainebleau of 1685. In 1686, Protestants comprised just 1% of the population.

The Huguenots were concentrated in the southern and western parts of the Kingdom of France. As Huguenots gained influence and more openly displayed their faith, Catholic hostility grew. A series of religious conflicts followed, known as the French Wars of Religion, fought intermittently from 1562 to 1598. The Huguenots were led by Jeanne d'Albret; her son, the future Henry IV (who would later convert to Catholicism in order to become king); and the princes of Condé. The wars ended with the Edict of Nantes of 1598, which granted the Huguenots substantial religious, political and military autonomy.

Huguenot rebellions in the 1620s resulted in the abolition of their political and military privileges. They retained the religious provisions of the Edict of Nantes until the rule of Louis XIV, who gradually increased persecution of Protestantism until he issued the Edict of Fontainebleau (1685). This ended legal recognition of Protestantism in France and the Huguenots were forced to either convert to Catholicism (possibly as Nicodemites) or flee as refugees; they were subject to violent Dragonnades. Louis XIV claimed the French Huguenot population was reduced from about 900,000 or 800,000 adherents to just 1,000 or 1,500. He exaggerated the decline, but the Dragonnades were devastating for the French Protestant community. The exodus of Huguenots from France created a brain drain, as many of them had occupied important places in society.

The remaining Huguenots faced continued persecution under Louis XV. By the time of his death in 1774, Calvinism had been all but eliminated from France. Persecution of Protestants officially ended with the Edict of Versailles, signed by Louis XVI in 1787. Two years later, with the Revolutionary Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen of 1789, Protestants gained equal rights as citizens.

A term used originally in derision, Huguenot has unclear origins. Various hypotheses have been promoted. The term may have been a combined reference to the Swiss politician Besançon Hugues (died 1532) and the religiously conflicted nature of Swiss republicanism in his time. It used a derogatory pun on the name Hugues by way of the Dutch word Huisgenoten (literally 'housemates'), referring to the connotations of a somewhat related word in German Eidgenosse ('Confederate' in the sense of 'a citizen of one of the states of the Swiss Confederacy').

In Geneva, John Calvin 's adopted home and the centre of the Calvinist movement, Hugues, though Catholic, was a leader of the "Confederate Party", so called because it favoured independence from the Duke of Savoy. It sought an alliance between the city-state of Geneva and the Swiss Confederation. ## Comparison: Huguenots (Britannica vs. Wikipedia)

**Bottom line:** The two sources agree on the core definition — Huguenots were French Protestants of the Reformed (Calvinist) tradition, and the name was originally a term of contempt/derision. Beyond that, they differ radically in scope. The Britannica entry is a two-sentence dictionary-style definition (156 characters, 12 tokens) that appears truncated by OCR, while the Wikipedia article is a comprehensive ~70,000-character entry covering etymology, demographics, geography, wars, edicts, persecution, exile, and eventual emancipation. The saved word-frequency comparison backs this up: Jaccard overlap of top terms is only 0.047, frequency cosine 0.296, and Wikipedia is roughly 500 times longer than Britannica (length ratio 501.5).

### What they agree on
- **Identity:** Britannica calls them "the reformed or Protestant Calvinists of France" [Britannica E0115, scan page `britannica:309f765b1ecc83e0a7f7762e44b4a927a7555443:train:1327`]. Wikipedia: "a religious group of French Protestants who held to the Reformed (Calvinist) tradition of Protestantism" [Wikipedia page 75899, revision 1352397655].
- **Contemptuous origin of the name:** Britannica: "an appellation given by way of contempt" [Britannica E0115]. Wikipedia: "A term used originally in derision" [Wikipedia page 75899, revision 1352397655].

### What Britannica says (limited)
- "HUGUENOTS, an appellation given by way of contempt to the reformed or Protestant Calvinists of France. The name had its first rise in 1560; but authors are" [Britannica E0115; text cuts off mid-sentence, and only 12 tokens were indexed, so this is a fragment].

### What Wikipedia adds (absent from the visible Britannica text)
- **Etymology hypotheses:** possibly from Genevan burgomaster Besançon Hugues, with a derogatory pun via Dutch *Huisgenoten* ("housemates") and German *Eidgenosse* ("Confederate") [Wikipedia page 75899, revision 1352397655].
- **Demographics:** up to ~10% of France on the eve of the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre (1572); 7–8% by 1600; just 1% by 1686, citing Hans Hillerbrand's *Encyclopedia of Protestantism* [Wikipedia page 75899, revision 1352397655].
- **Geography:** concentrated in southern and western France; eastern France (Alsace, Moselle, Montbéliard) was mainly Lutheran [Wikipedia page 75899, revision 1352397655].
- **Wars and edicts:** French Wars of Religion (1562–1598); leaders Jeanne d'Albret, Henry IV, princes of Condé; Edict of Nantes (1598) granted autonomy; Huguenot rebellions of the 1620s ended political/military privileges [Wikipedia page 75899, revision 1352397655].
- **Persecution and exile:** Louis XIV's Dragonnades and Edict of Fontainebleau (1685) ended legal recognition; Huguenots forced to convert or flee as refugees, creating a "brain drain"; Louis XIV claimed adherents fell from ~800,000–900,000 to 1,000–1,500 (an exaggeration) [Wikipedia page 75899, revision 1352397655].
- **Later emancipation:** persecution continued under Louis XV; Edict of Versailles (1787) ended official persecution; 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man gave Protestants equal rights [Wikipedia page 75899, revision 1352397655].

### Caveats
- The Britannica text is OCR'd and visibly incomplete — it ends mid-sentence ("but authors are") and comprises only 12 indexed tokens, so I cannot claim what a complete Britannica entry would say. The match to Wikipedia is accepted (title similarity 1.0), so both describe the same subject.
